OK, I get the whole "Spin a bucket of water" approach of creating centripetal force to simulate gravity for long-term space flights.

Rendezvous With Rama, Ender's Game, 2001: A Space Odyssey, Mission to Mars, and quite a few other books and movies have shown this time and again; the craft is designed with a large rotating ring or cylinder, people stand inside the craft with their feet on the inside of the rotating surface, and the centripetal force causes an effect similar to gravity, turning the entire inside diameter into a continuous floor. Got it.

But here's where it gets fuzzy for me:

In Rendezvous, The Southern plain was being explored in a nifty little flying machine. The pilot was told to stay near the axis of rotation, because 'gravity' would increase as he drifted away from the axis. And, as it turns out, he ended up crashing because he drifted too far from the center of rotation (I know, the lightning didn't help!) Arthur C. Clarke always seemed to be pretty accurate with things scientific, but I just don't see it happening this way.

Would there actually be any force to create the gravity effect on a person / object who was NOT standing inside the rotating surface?

I would think a person starting at the central axis could drift around through the craft fairly easily until they got to the 'floor' which would be spinning past them pretty quickly (coriolis effect); crashing into the floor would, as far as I can tell, result in them being scraped along the floor until they sped up and matched the lateral speed. But would they actually experience the artificial gravity without being physically in contact with the floor?

Thanks

The short answer is "no." Spin-induced artificial gravity is dependent on the person spinning along with the cylinder/ring, with (as you noted) the centripetal force simulating the effects of gravity. Within such a person's frame of reference, they are stationary WRT the cylinder itself and moving with regards to the rest of the universe, but stopped from flying down into it by the upward force of the cylinder on their feet. If they are stationary WRT the rest of the universe, the cylinder is now rotating with regards to them - if we could magically drop them onto a point inside the body of the cylinder, they wouldn't "feel" any gravity at all.

In reality, though, things would work a little bit differently for one simple reason: they cylinder is probably full of air, which is rotating along with the cylinder. Thus, if you drop someone in near the center axis of the cylinder they won't feel much gravity or force, but once they're off the center axis the air will start to speed them up the same way being scraped along the floor would be (not as nastily though) and they'd start to be "pulled" towards the outside of the cylinder long before they synced up with it. Without running any numbers, my guess is that the overall outcome would be fairly situational (spin velocity, cylinder size etc), but it could potentially range from them slowly speeding up to match the cylinder while drifting floorwards and pretty much syncing neatly....to being promptly thrown into the floor as though they'd fallen from a significant height.
